title: What Is the Tough White Strip in a Chicken Tenderloin, and Should You Remove It?

seo.title: White Strip in Chicken Tenderloin: Tendon or Something Else?
seo.meta_description: The tough white cord running through a chicken tenderloin is usually a tendon. It is normal anatomy and edible, but it can stay chewy after cooking, so trimming is optional.
seo.search_intent: Identify the white cord in chicken tenderloins and decide whether removing it improves texture or safety.

excerpt: The firm white cord through a chicken tenderloin is normally a tendon connecting muscle to bone. It is not a worm or plastic and does not need removal for food safety, but it can remain tough after cooking, so many cooks trim it for texture.
content_html:
The tough white cord running through a chicken tenderloin is usually a tendon, a normal piece of connective tissue that helps attach the small breast muscle to the skeleton. It is not a parasite, a plastic strand, or evidence that something went wrong during processing.

The tendon is edible and does not have to be removed for safety. The reason cooks often pull or trim it out is texture: collagen-rich tendon can remain noticeably firmer and chewier than the tender muscle around it, especially with quick cooking.

The tenderloin is a small muscle with a prominent connective attachment

Chicken tenderloin is the smaller pectoral muscle lying underneath the larger breast. Like other muscles, it needs connective tissue to transmit force to the skeleton. The pale cord you see is part of that attachment system.

Raw tendon is white because dense collagen reflects light differently from the pink muscle tissue. It may run through a substantial portion of the tenderloin and become especially obvious when the meat is separated from the main breast.

The cord can feel slippery and elastic when raw. Once heated, collagen proteins tighten and change, but a quick sauté or fry does not necessarily soften a thick tendon enough to make it disappear.

Leaving it in changes texture more than safety

If you cook the tenderloin whole, the tendon can create a stringy, rubbery strip through an otherwise tender bite. Some people barely notice it, while others find the contrast unpleasant. The effect is strongest in larger tenderloins with a thick cord.

Long, moist cooking can soften connective tissue more than a brief high-heat method, although chicken tenderloins are so lean and small that cooking them for a very long time may dry the muscle before the tendon becomes luxurious and gelatinous.

Removing the tendon does not sanitize the chicken. Raw poultry still requires careful hand washing practices, avoidance of cross-contamination, refrigeration, and cooking to a safe internal temperature.

There are several ways to remove the tendon

The simplest method is to expose the thick end with a small knife, hold it with a paper towel for grip, and scrape or slice the meat away while pulling gently. The goal is to remove the cord without taking a large amount of tenderloin with it.

A popular fork method traps the tendon between fork tines while it is pulled through, but results vary. If the cord tears or the meat starts shredding, stop and use a knife rather than sacrificing the shape of the whole piece.

You do not need to chase every tiny white thread. Fine connective tissue runs throughout muscle naturally. Removing the prominent central tendon is mainly a preparation choice for a smoother bite.

Do not confuse normal tendon with spoilage signs

A clean white cord inside firm raw chicken is expected anatomy. Spoilage looks different: persistent foul odor, tacky slime, leaking damaged packaging, or meat held under unsafe conditions. The tendon itself does not cause those changes.

Color can vary with lighting, packaging, and muscle differences, so no single white feature should be interpreted without context. If the chicken has been properly stored and the only unusual feature is a firm internal cord, tendon is the likely explanation.

Tenderloin preparation also depends on the final dish. For skewers, quick stir-fries, or breaded strips, removing a thick tendon can keep the piece from curling and prevent one chewy cord from dominating a small portion. If the meat will be minced for meatballs, chopped for a filling, or shredded after slow cooking, the benefit is much smaller because the connective tissue is divided into short pieces. Chilling the tenderloin well before trimming can make the tendon easier to grip and keeps the meat firmer under the knife. Work on a clean board reserved for raw poultry and wash hands and tools afterward. The popular tendon-removal tricks are therefore culinary techniques, not sanitation procedures; the food-safety controls remain separation from ready-to-eat foods, refrigeration, and adequate cooking.

You can safely leave the tendon in, but removing it often improves eating quality. Treat it like a piece of connective tissue rather than a contaminant: trim when its chewiness would bother you, and focus food-safety attention on refrigeration, clean handling, and thorough cooking.

faq.question: Is the white string in chicken tenderloin a worm?
faq.answer: No. It is normally a tendon, a collagen-rich connective structure belonging to the chicken.

faq.question: Is chicken tendon safe to eat?
faq.answer: Yes. It is normal connective tissue, although it can remain chewy after quick cooking.

faq.question: Do I have to remove the tendon?
faq.answer: No. Removal is optional and mainly improves texture and presentation.
